title: The Vishwakarma sector: workers who are not employees
author: Editorial Desk
summary: BMS's term for self-employed craftspeople who are neither employer nor employee, how big the group is, and what the PM Vishwakarma Scheme offers.
body:
Labour law was written with two figures in mind: an employer and an employee. But millions of Indians are neither. A potter, a weaver, a carpenter, a blacksmith, a cobbler or a goldsmith owns his tools, decides how to do the work and sells either the product or the skill. There is no employer to pay a provident fund, to give a notice period or to be taken to a labour court. BMS calls this large group the **Vishwakarma sector**. This post explains the idea, the scale of the group it describes and the government scheme that carries the same name.

## A word for a missing category

Classical labour thinking, in the form that reached India, pictured society as two sides, with capital on one and wage labour on the other. Trade union law, wage law and social security law followed that picture. A person who was neither a capitalist nor a wage earner did not fit, and so was often left outside the protection of any law.

An Organiser article on BMS at 70 says that BMS introduced the Vishwakarma sector as a way of recognising self-employed skilled workers, whom, in its view, Marxist frameworks never accommodated, and that such workers are now a recognised category in international discussion. We could not find a primary text of the idea in the sources we consulted, so we present it as BMS's own account. The same article says that BMS observes 17 September, Vishwakarma Day, as National Labour Day. The choice of the name follows from that: in Indian tradition, Vishwakarma is the patron of those who work with their hands and tools, a point developed in the next post.

According to the usual description, the people of the Vishwakarma sector are **self-employed, skilled and traditional**. Their skill is often passed down in the family, so that a child learns the trade at the side of a parent, and their work forms the backbone of the artisan economy.

## How big is the group?

Nobody knows exactly, because the definition is not fixed, but the surrounding figures give some sense of scale.

- The Periodic Labour Force Survey for 2023-24 found that **58.4 per cent** of India's workers were self-employed, up from 57.3 per cent the year before. That figure includes unpaid family workers and small businesses of all kinds, so it is much wider than the artisan group, but it shows how common work without an employer is. Regular wage or salaried workers were only 21.7 per cent.
- The Fourth All-India Handloom Census, conducted in 2019-20, counted **35,22,512 persons** engaged in handloom weaving and related work. That is just one craft.
- An Organiser article says the unorganised sector makes up about 90 per cent of the workforce.

If a country's labour policy is designed only for the employer-employee relationship, then it covers a minority of working people.

## What the sector needs

- **Credit and raw materials** at fair terms. A craftsperson who borrows from a moneylender to buy raw materials, and sells to a middleman, loses most of the value of their work.
- **Markets** for their products, and protection from cheap imitations. Handmade goods compete with factory goods, and buyers rarely see the person who made them.
- **Skill upgrading** and tools. Traditional skills do not stay still, and tools and design need updating.
- **Social security**, since no employer pays their provident fund. A weaver or a mason who is injured, ill or old has no pension or insurance unless a scheme supplies it.
- **Recognition**, in the form of a certificate or card, so that the person can show that he is an artisan and claim benefits.

## A policy echo: the PM Vishwakarma Scheme

On **17 September 2023**, which is Vishwakarma Jayanti, the Union Government launched the **PM Vishwakarma Scheme** for traditional artisans and craftspeople, at the Yashobhoomi centre in Dwarka, New Delhi. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs had approved it on 16 August 2023. The details, as published, are as follows.

- It is a central sector scheme under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, with an outlay of **Rs 13,000 crore** for the five years from 2023-24 to 2027-28.
- It covers **18 traditional trades**: carpenter, boat maker, armourer, blacksmith, hammer and tool kit maker, locksmith, goldsmith, potter, sculptor, stone breaker, cobbler or footwear artisan, mason, basket, mat and broom maker or coir weaver, doll and toy maker, barber, garland maker, washerman, tailor and fishing net maker.
- Benefits include a PM Vishwakarma certificate and ID card, skill training with a stipend of Rs 500 a day, a toolkit incentive of up to Rs 15,000, collateral-free credit of up to Rs 1 lakh and then Rs 2 lakh at a concessional interest rate of 5 per cent, an incentive for digital transactions, and support for marketing.
- Eligible people must be aged above 18, working with their hands and tools in one of the trades on a self-employed basis, and only one member of a family may benefit. Government employees and their families are excluded.
- As of January 2025, **26.87 lakh** beneficiaries had been registered, against a target the Communications Minister described as more than 30 lakh families.

Whatever the details, the choice of name reflects an idea that BMS had long promoted: that the self-employed artisan is a worker, with a claim on the nation's attention. There are also debates about the scheme. The Organiser piece notes that some commentators on the Left attacked it for reinforcing caste-based occupations, and the Tribune report notes that it is aimed chiefly at OBC, SC and ST communities in traditional rural trades. Supporters answer that it supports skills that families already have, and does not prevent anyone from choosing another livelihood. Both views deserve to be heard, and the results in time will show which concerns are borne out.

## What a policy for this sector would look like

Seen from the standpoint of the sector, the scheme leaves several questions open. Does the loan reach those who cannot offer collateral? Do the toolkits match what a craftsperson actually needs? Is there a market at the end of the training? And does a certificate lead on to a pension and an insurance cover, or only to a loan? These are the points that federations working among artisans can follow up, and they are among the reasons why a labour organisation, and not only a Ministry, needs to be in the conversation.

## The principle

A good labour policy begins by looking at how people really work. Workers come in more forms than one law can describe, and a country with tens of millions of self-employed people has to design protection that fits them. The Vishwakarma sector is BMS's name for that task.
